passages.t: Grumbling in the Desert of Sin
passages.happening:
“On the fifteenth day of the second month after they had left the land of Egypt, the whole congregation of Israel set out from Elim and came to the Desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai” (verse 1).

“And there in the desert they all grumbled against Moses and Aaron” (verse 2).

“‘If only we had died by the LORD’s hand in the land of Egypt!’ they said. ‘There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread, but you have brought us into this desert to starve this whole assembly to death!’” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
It is one month since they left Egypt. The food they carried out has run out.

The Desert of Sin is a place name. It has nothing to do with the English word ‘sin’. It lay between Elim and Mount Sinai, somewhere in the Sinai Peninsula. Exactly where depends on where Sinai was, which is itself debated.

At the sea God rescued them from Pharaoh. At Marah he made bitter water sweet. Now the desert asks a harder question. Can God be trusted not just for one great rescue, but for every day's food?

Listen to the complaint. ‘Pots of meat.’ ‘Our fill of bread.’ Even slaves on Egypt's building works were given rations. In the desert there is nothing. And so slavery begins to look like safety. It is a very human thing to remember the past as better than it was.

Notice too who they grumble against: Moses and Aaron. Moses will soon tell them who they are really grumbling against.
passages.later:
Israel kept grumbling on the road. Numbers tells it: “We remember the fish we ate freely in Egypt, along with the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic” (Numbers 11:5).

Paul warns the church from these stories: “Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness. These things took place as examples” (1 Corinthians 10:5-6).
passages.asks: In hunger, Egypt began to look good again. Ask whether there is an old life you remember as better than it really was. And ask what it would mean to bring your hunger to God instead of grumbling against those around you.

passages.t: ‘I will rain down bread from heaven’
passages.happening:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Behold, I will rain down bread from heaven for you. Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day. In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions’” (verse 4). On the sixth day they will gather twice as much (verse 5).

Moses and Aaron tell the people, “in the morning you will see the LORD’s glory, because He has heard your grumbling against Him. For who are we that you should grumble against us?” (verse 7). “Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD” (verse 8).

As Aaron speaks, “they looked toward the desert, and there in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared” (verse 10). God says, “At twilight you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
God answers the grumbling, first of all, with bread. Not with punishment. The people complained, and God says, ‘I have heard’.

But the bread comes with a test. Gather only enough for each day. Trust that tomorrow's food will come tomorrow. It is a daily lesson in depending on God.

‘Who are we?’ Moses and Aaron step out of the way. The people's complaint is really against the LORD, because he is the one who brought them out. That is not said to shame them. It is said so that they will turn to the one who can actually help.

Then the glory appears in the cloud. The God who heard is present, right there in the desert.
passages.later:
The psalm remembers: “He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven. Man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 78:24-25).

In John 6, after Jesus feeds a crowd, people say, “Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat’” (John 6:31). Jesus answers, “it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven” (John 6:32).
passages.asks: God answered complaint with bread, and with a daily test of trust. Ask what you are anxious about for tomorrow. And ask what it would look like to gather only what you need for today, and trust God for the rest.

passages.t: Quail, manna, and enough for each day
passages.happening:
“That evening quail came and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp” (verse 13). When the dew lifts, “there were thin flakes on the desert floor, as fine as frost on the ground” (verse 14).

“When the Israelites saw it, they asked one another, ‘What is it?’ For they did not know what it was. So Moses told them, ‘It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat’” (verse 15).

Each gathers what he needs. “When they measured it by the omer, he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall” (verse 18).

“No one may keep any of it until morning”, Moses says. Some do not listen, “and it became infested with maggots and began to smell” (verses 19-20). “Every morning each one gathered as much as was needed, and when the sun grew hot, it melted away” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The name ‘manna’ comes from the people's question. In Hebrew ‘What is it?’ is man hu. The bread is named after their puzzlement.

An omer was a measure, here said to be a tenth of an ephah. Ancient measures are hard to fix exactly, but it is usually reckoned at roughly two litres, a generous day's food for one person.

Notice the strange fairness of it. Some gathered more and some less, but when it was measured, everyone had enough. No one had too much, and no one went short.

And notice the test. Some tried to save it for tomorrow. It went bad. God's daily bread cannot be stored up against God. It must be trusted for each day.
passages.later:
Moses later explains the lesson of the manna: “He humbled you, and in your hunger He gave you manna to eat”, he says, “so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3). Jesus quotes it in his own wilderness testing (Matthew 4:4).

Paul quotes verse 18 to urge Christians to share with one another: “He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall” (2 Corinthians 8:15).

Jesus taught his disciples to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11).
passages.hard:
Was the manna a natural substance or a miracle?

Two things found in Sinai have been compared with this account. Quail fly across the peninsula in spring and autumn, and tired flocks can come down in great numbers where they land. And certain small insects feeding on tamarisk trees in Sinai produce a sweet, sticky drop that hardens into small white beads in the cool of the morning. Local people have gathered it and call it by the Arabic word man.

So some readers see God's provision working through the natural world he made, as the east wind worked at the sea. Others note that the natural substance comes only in small amounts and only in certain seasons, while Exodus describes enough food for the whole people every day for forty years, a double portion on the sixth day, none on the seventh, and spoiling that stops for the Sabbath. They conclude the text describes a miracle no natural product explains. A third group of scholars treats the account as a later tradition that turned a desert food into a picture of God's care.

These notes do not choose. The chapter's own interest is plain: whatever the means, the food came from God, and it came in a way that taught Israel to trust him one day at a time.
passages.asks: Everyone had enough, and no one had too much. Ask whether you are gathering more than you need while others go short. And ask what it would look like to share so that, around you, ‘he who gathered little had no shortfall’.

passages.t: The Sabbath, a gift of rest
passages.happening:
On the sixth day they gather twice as much (verse 22). Moses tells them, “This is what the LORD has said: ‘Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD’” (verse 23). They keep it until morning, “and it did not smell or contain any maggots” (verse 24).

“For six days you may gather, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, it will not be there” (verse 26). Yet some go out on the seventh day, “but they did not find anything” (verse 27).

God says, “How long will you refuse to keep My commandments and instructions? Understand that the LORD has given you the Sabbath; that is why on the sixth day He will give you bread for two days” (verses 28-29). “So the people rested on the seventh day” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
This is the first time the Sabbath is given to Israel as a command. Genesis already tells of God resting on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2-3). Now God's people are given a share in his rest, before the law has even been given at Sinai.

Think of who receives it. People who have just come out of forced labor, where the work never stopped. Now they are given a day when they must not work, and God provides the food for it in advance. A regular day of rest for everyone, slaves included, was unusual in the ancient world.

Notice the words in verse 29: ‘the LORD has given you the Sabbath’. It comes first as a gift. Some still went out to gather. They could not quite believe they were allowed to stop.
passages.later:
Jesus says, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

Hebrews speaks of a rest still ahead for God's people: “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9).

Paul writes, “let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16-17), and “One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (Romans 14:5).
passages.hard:
Should Christians keep a Sabbath today? Christians differ, and each main view should be stated as its holders would.

Seventh-day Christians, among them Seventh Day Baptists and Seventh-day Adventists, hold that the command to rest on the seventh day still stands as given, since Jesus kept the Sabbath and the rest is rooted in creation, before Israel existed. The Reformed and Puritan tradition, set out in the Westminster Confession (1646), holds that the Sabbath principle continues, moved by Christ's resurrection to the first day of the week as the Lord's Day. Catholic, Lutheran and many other Christians hold that the moral heart of the commandments is permanent, while the seventh-day rest was a sign fulfilled in Christ, and they keep Sunday as the day of resurrection; Luther read the commandment chiefly as a call to hear God's word. And some, in dispensational and New Covenant traditions, hold that the covenant of Moses as a whole has been fulfilled in Christ, pointing to Colossians 2:16-17 and Romans 14:5.

All of these agree that rest is God's good gift, and that it is not a way of earning his favor. They differ over how God's covenant with Israel relates to the church. These notes take no side. And this chapter speaks to all of them: before it was a rule, the Sabbath was bread given in advance and a day off for a people who had never had one.
passages.asks: Some went out to gather on the day of rest; they could not believe they were allowed to stop. Ask whether you find it hard to rest, as if everything depends on you. And ask what it would look like to receive rest as a gift from the God who provides.

passages.t: A jar of manna for the generations
passages.happening:
“Now the house of Israel called the bread manna. It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey” (verse 31).

God commands, “Keep an omer of manna for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt” (verse 32). Aaron puts a jar of it “in front of the Testimony, to be preserved” (verse 34).

“The Israelites ate manna forty years, until they came to a land where they could settle; they ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Coriander seed is small and round. Manna was white, and sweet like wafers made with honey.

A jar of it is kept so that later generations can see what God gave. Israel's faith is a remembering faith.

‘The Testimony’ means the tablets of the covenant kept in the ark. They have not yet been given at this point in the story. The verse looks ahead to a later practice. These closing verses step outside the story's time, to the forty years of manna and the generations to come. The chapter was written to teach later readers as well as to tell what happened.
passages.later:
The manna stopped when Israel reached the land: “And the day after they had eaten from the produce of the land, the manna ceased” (Joshua 5:12).

Hebrews describes the ark: “Inside the ark were the gold jar of manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the stone tablets of the covenant” (Hebrews 9:4).

Jesus says, “Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die. I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:49-51).
passages.asks: A jar of manna was kept so that later generations would see what God provided. Ask what reminders of God's care you keep, in your home or in your memory. And ask whether you have told the next generation about the daily bread God has given you.
